author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: A Nail from the Commonwealth
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
The new fastener looked perfect until I pulled it from the board.

Orange rust coated the threads. The metal was rough where it should have been smooth, and the hole in the timber had widened enough for seawater to gather around it.

Maui stared at it.

"That came from Danse. I'm going to have a very dignified conversation with him. By which I mean pointing at this rust until it apologizes."

"From Brasswatch," I corrected. "It might have come through his workshop. That doesn't make it his fault."

"It was supposed to last."

"So was the old rope."

Fen examined the piece under a magnifying lens. We'd found it during the morning inspection at the lower landing, where Lio's skiff had begun knocking against a repair bracket. Nobody had been injured. We had taken the mooring out of service immediately.

Tamsin joined us with the purchase record.

"Salvage fastener," she read. "Recovered from a dry storage shed in the Commonwealth. Inspected for shape and load."

"Not for salt," Fen said.

Tamsin closed her eyes.

"Not for salt."

Maui folded his arms. "Why didn't anyone check?"

I looked at him.

He winced. "Right. That's the question. Not the accusation."

We carried the rusted nail to Brasswatch.

Danse was teaching Renn how to test a water pump. He took one look at the fastener and put the training piece aside.

"That's not acceptable," he said.

"Can you tell us why?" I asked.

He turned the nail under the light.

"Corrosion. The protective coating was already compromised. Dry use might not have exposed it quickly, but coastal spray would."

Toph arrived from the next workroom, following the sound of our conversation.

"Something's wrong with the dock?"

"One bracket," Tamsin said. "The rest is being inspected."

Toph held the fastener carefully, testing its weight. "This isn't magic, is it?"

Danse looked offended. "No."

"Good. I hate when people make bad engineering interesting by calling it a curse."

Renn fetched the batch ledger. There were twelve nails from the same salvaged lot. Five had been used at Tideglass, three on a protected shed in Brasswatch, and four remained in storage.

"We need all of them identified," Danse said.

Maui looked toward the door. "I'll go tear them out."

His hook was already in his hand. For one horrible instant I could picture him ripping half the pier to pieces in pursuit of a problem that was holding the other half up.

"Great Maui to the rescue," he announced through clenched teeth. "One hundred rusty nails, zero survivors."

"Five installed here," Danse corrected, looking at the ledger. "Twelve in the batch."

"You're ruining the rhythm."

Mini Maui appeared beside the hook tattoo and drew a small diagram of a collapsing dock. The larger Maui stared at it, then at the real water below the window.

"Okay, yes," he muttered. "Maybe not the whole dock."

He had extraordinary strength and absolutely no patience for watching a problem become a spreadsheet. The waiting made him twitch. Yet when Tamsin asked him to brace a beam while she checked the replacement, he planted himself there and held it as steadily as a mountain.

"Just so we're clear," he told me, "I am still the strongest person here."

"Nobody disputed that."

"Good. Because I needed to hear it."

He grinned. The grin was not an apology for being wrong. The decision to wait was.

"Not all at once," Tamsin said. "Some are holding things in place until we brace the structure."

He stopped.

We made a list of locations and assigned inspection teams. Fen closed the affected landing section. Tamsin designed temporary supports. Danse checked the material specification and compared replacement options. Renn contacted the supplier without accusing them of fraud; the material had been sold for general salvage, not coastal structural service.

The supplier replied that afternoon. They had no evidence the pieces had been rated for salt exposure.

It was a mistake, not a conspiracy.

I could see Maui struggling with that.

"A villain would be easier," he admitted while we waited for the new hardware. "You fight them. You win. Everyone gets a safe dock."

"Instead we have paperwork."

"An evil thing."

I laughed.

Renn had another question before we ordered replacements.

"How do we know the next lot is actually what the label claims?"

It was the sort of question I was embarrassed not to have asked. Danse put down the faulty fastener and looked at the supplier's old order sheet.

"We should have checked the material specification against the conditions at Tideglass," he admitted. "A second invoice isn't a test."

Tamsin suggested separating the remaining salvaged stock into marked bins: dry interior use, pending verification, and unsafe. Fen wanted the rejected lot traced to its origin without claiming a faulty batch proved malicious intent. Lio wanted to know whether the temporary closure would cost the small boat crews an entire day of work.

"Not if we schedule the repairs around the safe tide window," Fen said. "But they'll need notice."

I wrote the closure times on a draft sign. Edda, who had come to deliver a route report, looked at it and pointed out that the detour described a set of steps without naming an accessible alternative. I added the upper path and asked her to test the directions on the ground before we posted them.

Maui watched the growing list.

"Is there anything about this nail that doesn't involve a committee?"

"Yes," Danse said. "It fails in salt water."

Toph barked a laugh. So did I.

The new order listed the actual corrosion rating, the use conditions, and a person responsible for checking the certificate before installation. We set aside money for labor rather than asking the repair crew to donate its afternoon. I wanted the change to look more impressive than a receipt. It didn't.

It would, however, keep the next person from having to pull rust out of the same board while pretending nobody could have known.

The replacement fasteners cost more. They had a suitable corrosion rating and came with a maintenance schedule. Mara agreed to cover part of the immediate cost from the repair fund; the remaining expense went to the next council meeting instead of disappearing into someone's unpaid time.

We worked in daylight. Fen supervised the lift. Lio held a support while the first bracket came free. Maui braced the timber without taking over the job. Danse and Tamsin checked the fit. Toph tested the movement through the stone foundation and reported what she could feel, without pretending she could inspect the metal's internal condition.

When the first replacement passed, we cheered.

Then we tested four more.

By sunset the mooring was usable again at a reduced load. The final load test would happen after the next tide cycle. We posted the restriction at the landing in large letters.

Maui looked at the sign.

"Does everything here come with conditions?"

"Anything worth keeping does," Fen said.

I thought about the relationship agreement on our kitchen table. That had conditions too: honesty, choice, the ability to revise. It hadn't made our affection less real.

Danse washed his hands at the work sink.

"I authorized the first batch for use," he said. "I'll document where I failed to check the environment."

Tamsin looked at him.

"I approved the installation."

"And I carried the materials," Maui added.

Fen nodded. "Then the report will show what each of you did. Nobody benefits if you turn the record into a competition for blame."

Renn wrote the final note. Their handwriting was small and tidy.

At dinner, the group ate fish soup by the sheltered garden. Danse stayed for one bowl before returning to Brasswatch. Iroh sent tea from Jasmine Steps. Greg arrived late and asked whether the dock was going to make a dramatic noise again.

"Not if we can help it," I said.

He looked faintly disappointed.

When everyone left, Maui held the corroded nail in his palm.

"We should keep it," he said.

"Why?"

"So I remember to ask what a thing was made for, not just whether I can lift it."

We set it on the shelf beneath the tide chart, in a little clear jar labeled *Not for the sea.*

Maui leaned toward me.

"Can I kiss you before you make another label?"

"Yes."

He kissed me until I forgot what I'd been about to write. Later I found the pencil under the table and laughed.

The next morning Fen's report came back: the tide test had passed within the posted limits.

The jar remained where we could see it.

Not every failure deserved a legend. Some deserved the right replacement part and the humility to read its specification.
